title: Post-Cataract Surgery Complications: The Master Clinical Roadmap
summary: An exhaustive guide to identifying and managing post-cataract surgical complications, ranging from posterior capsule rupture to endophthalmitis. This poster integrates incidence statistics, intraoperative management protocols, and clinical pearls for the anterior segment surgeon.

sections.title: Signs of Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR)
content: Sudden deepening or shallowing of the Anterior Chamber (AC)
Momentary pupillary dilation
Nucleus falls away and cannot be approached by phaco tip
Marked slowing of aspiration due to clogged vitreous in phaco tip
Torn capsule may be directly visible
Vitreous gel may be directly visible

sections.title: Sequelae of Vitreous Loss after PCR
PCR Management: Core Principles
content: Management depends on the magnitude of the tear
Depends on the size and type of any residual lens material
Depends on the presence or absence of vitreous prolapse
CRITICAL: Do NOT pull out the phaco probe immediately (maintains AC pressure)

sections.title: PCR Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Inject dispersive viscoelastic before removing phaco probe
Step 2: If a complete or nearly complete nucleus remains, convert to ECCE
Step 3: If residual nuclear fragments, remove by phaco using low bottle height and low aspiration flow rate
Step 4: If large fragments, use visco-expression after extending the main wound
Step 5: Once remnants are removed, replug the tear with dispersive OVD
Step 6: Gently fill the AC with cohesive viscoelastic
Step 7: Use manual aspiration cannula with irrigation OFF to aspirate residual cortex
Step 8: Remove all vitreous from AC, wound, and capsular tear with a vitrector
Step 9: Infusion cannula of vitrector remains HIGH; Cutter remains LOW
Step 10: Visualize vitreous using 0.1 ml of 40mg/ml Triamcinolone

rows: Constrict pupil following PC IOL or prior to AC IOL

sections.title: Clinical Complications: Continuous List
sections.content: Additional complications noted include: Corneal decompensation, chronic endophthalmitis, and specific post-operative inflammation rates ranging from 2% to 6%. PCO remains a primary late complication at 10% within 2 years.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Post-Op Vision Loss

rows: Immediate onset (12-24h), no pain, limbus-to-limbus edema
Elevated IOP, corneal edema, mid-dilated pupil
Loss of red reflex, sudden pain, AC shallowing

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Endophthalmitis (0.1%): Immediate referral if pain/hypopyon present
Choroidal Haemorrhage (0.1%): Intraoperative disaster requiring immediate wound closure
Loss of nuclear fragment posteriorly (0.3%): Requires vitreoretinal consultation
Wound leak (1%): Risk for hypotony and endophthalmitis
Iris Prolapse (0.7%): Requires surgical repair to prevent infection

content.explanation: D: Deepening/shallowing of AC. R: Red reflex change/loss. O: Out of reach nucleus (falls away). P: Pupil dilation (momentary).

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Vitreous Visualization
content: Always use preservative-free Triamcinolone (0.1ml of 40mg/ml) to stain vitreous strands.
Stained vitreous appears as white specks trapped in the gel, making clean-up far more precise.
Ensure AC is stable with OVD before starting the vitrectomy cutter.
